No, almost certainly not. With six people, microservices mostly add cost: network failure modes, distributed transactions, per-service deploy and observability overhead, and a platform burden that would consume a meaningful share of your engineering time. The benefits (independent team deploys, independent scaling, fault isolation) address problems that appear with many teams stepping on each other, which you don't have.

If the monolith hurts, the cheaper fixes are usually a modular monolith (Packwerk or Rails engines to enforce boundaries), background job queues for heavy work, read replicas and caching, and fixing the specific slow paths. These keep one deploy and one database while giving you most of the structural benefit.

The strongest case for splitting is a specific component with genuinely different needs, such as a workload needing different scaling or language/runtime (ML inference, video processing), a hard compliance isolation requirement (PCI, PHI), or a part that must stay up when the rest fails. Extract that one piece as a single service; don't decompose the whole app.

What would flip this: team growth past roughly 30-50 engineers with deploy contention or ownership conflicts, or a measured bottleneck that modularization and scaling the monolith can't solve. If you're considering it because of a specific pain (slow deploys, slow tests, tangled code, scaling), tell me which and I can suggest a targeted fix.
